source_spans.locator: Cognitive Psychology 19(1), published pp.1-6, Abstract and Introduction: performance facilitation is distinguished from introspective report; the paper separately asks whether reduced focal processing prevents sequence acquisition and whether performance change can occur without awareness of the repeated pattern

Cognitive Psychology 19(1), published pp.6-10, Experiment 1: four-choice response task, fixed ten-position sequence versus random order; repeating-order response latency diverges from random within the first block and falls substantially across eight blocks

Cognitive Psychology 19(1), published pp.10-16, Experiment 2: single-repeating, dual-repeating, and dual-random groups; concurrent low-tone counting; four 100-trial exposure blocks followed by a two-block generate task; dual-repeating and dual-random latency functions do not significantly differ, while generate performance shows at most small residual prior-sequence benefit

Cognitive Psychology 19(1), published pp.16-21, Experiment 3: after four dual-repeating blocks, transfer to single-repeating versus single-random conditions; no significant initial repeating advantage and no faster relearning relative to previously unexposed single-repeating groups

Cognitive Psychology 19(1), published pp.21-27, Experiment 4: six Korsakoff patients and eight age-matched controls perform repeating then random blocks; both groups show practice-related response-time reduction and slowing when the order becomes random; serial-position analyses show qualitatively similar changing chunk patterns

Cognitive Psychology 19(1), published pp.26-27, Experiment 4 subjective reports: controls report the repeating pattern whereas Korsakoff patients do not, despite performance evidence that the patient group acquired the sequence

Cognitive Psychology 19(1), published pp.27-30, General Discussion: four converging comparisons support strong dependence of new sequence acquisition on focal processing allocation; dual-task practice still improves generic dual-task performance; awareness of the pattern is explicitly distinguished from attending to the task itself

conditions: a four-choice speeded response task containing either a fixed ten-position order or a constrained random order
performance conducted either alone or concurrently with a low-tone counting task that competes for focal processing resources
new order acquisition assessed by multiple performance and report surfaces rather than by practice-related speedup alone
population: University of Minnesota undergraduate participants in Experiments 1-3
six adults with Korsakoff's syndrome and eight age-matched healthy older adults in Experiment 4
task: press one of four spatially compatible keys in response to successive visual locations
under concurrent-task conditions also count low-pitched tones presented during the response-to-stimulus interval
temporal_scope: immediate post-exposure generation and transfer tests

nodes.description: whether successive visual locations follow the fixed ten-position order or a constrained random order
secondary task requiring a running count of low-pitched tones while performing the visual response task
amount of processing capacity available for the visual response task while another task is or is not performed concurrently
response-time benefit attributable specifically to experience with the fixed order, estimated by comparison with random-order performance rather than by raw practice speedup alone
response-time improvement across concurrent-task blocks that occurs for both fixed-order and random-order groups
comparison of response-latency functions between fixed-order and random-order conditions during repeated task performance
post-exposure task in which participants press the key corresponding to the location they expect to occur next and accuracy is measured
accuracy in predicting the next location after prior fixed-order or random-order exposure
removal of the concurrent tone task followed by fixed-order or random-order blocks to test immediate benefit and subsequent savings from prior concurrent fixed-order exposure
initial response-time advantage for the fixed order after concurrent-task exposure
faster subsequent acquisition of the fixed order attributable to earlier concurrent-task exposure
spontaneous and prompted report about whether a repeating order was noticed
report that a repeating order was present during task performance
Korsakoff patient group versus age-matched healthy control group in the fourth experiment
replacement of the fixed order by a random order after four fixed-order blocks
baseline-corrected response-time analysis across the ten serial positions used to characterize which portions of the fixed order were acquired
pattern of baseline-corrected response times across positions in the fixed order and its change with practice

relations.description: when the visual response task is performed alone, fixed-order and random-order response times diverge early and the fixed-order condition shows a much larger practice-related reduction
performing the tone-counting task concurrently is used to reduce the processing capacity available for the visual response task

under concurrent-task exposure, fixed-order and random-order groups do not significantly diverge in response latency across the four exposure blocks, unlike the rapid divergence observed when the task is performed alone

response latency nevertheless decreases with practice in both concurrent fixed-order and concurrent random-order groups, so generic improvement in handling the combined tasks is distinguished from fixed-order acquisition
fixed-order versus random-order latency comparison provides a performance measure of order-specific benefit rather than treating any reduction in raw latency as evidence of order acquisition
the post-exposure prediction task measures usable knowledge of the next location; prior single-task fixed-order exposure yields a larger initial advantage than prior concurrent fixed-order exposure
removing the concurrent task tests both immediate benefit from prior fixed-order exposure and whether the fixed order is reacquired faster than by previously unexposed comparison groups
four blocks of concurrent fixed-order exposure produce neither a significant initial fixed-order advantage after transfer nor detectable savings in subsequent fixed-order acquisition

after four fixed-order blocks, replacing the order with random locations produces a response-time increase in both the Korsakoff and healthy older groups, providing performance evidence for acquisition of the specific order
baseline-corrected serial-position response times reveal acquisition across much of the fixed order and a changing chunk-like profile with practice
the patient and healthy older groups show qualitatively similar serial-position patterns and similar changes in those patterns with practice, despite quantitative performance differences
spontaneous and prompted reports separately measure whether participants noticed the repeating order
performance evidence for acquisition can occur without a report that the repeating order was noticed, as shown most clearly by the Korsakoff group

acquisition of the new fixed-order associations is strongly reduced when processing capacity is divided across the two concurrent tasks, whereas noticing the existence of the order is not required for the performance benefit itself
